results.title: ChatGPT vs Claude for Real Work: What I Learned While Applying for an AI Job
results.content:
It’s the history.

I’ve been working with ChatGPT for about three years. That means there are hundreds of conversations connected to my projects, my writing, my podcast work, my LLM usage, and more recently my job search.

When I started working on the actual job application today, that history mattered.

ChatGPT already had the context of previous resumes, applications, and examples we’d worked through together. So continuing that work felt natural.

Trying to start the same process in Claude felt much slower.

Not because Claude is worse.

But because there’s no shared history yet. Well, 3 days so far, which is not enough right now.

It’s a bit like working with someone new on a project. Even if they’re excellent, you still have to explain everything again. [...] That said, I did find a workflow that helped today.

I worked on the job application inside ChatGPT. Once I had the core materials drafted there, I moved pieces of that work into Claude while outlining the new AI website I’m building. I didn’t realize these two tasks would complement each other so well but they did, so I leaned into it.

Since the website project was mostly new, it didn’t rely as heavily on existing conversations.

So the workflow looked something like this:

 ChatGPT for the ongoing work that already has history.
 Claude for the newer project where we’re starting fresh.

It actually worked quite well.

And it’s slowly helping me build up more context inside Claude. [...] There’s often a bit of explanation, context, framing, and then eventually a list.

Claude, on the other hand, tends to give me paragraphs more quickly. The answers come in a slightly more compact format.

> “For training humans to use AI: The terms recruiters use are AI Trainer, AI Educator, AI Literacy Coach, or Prompt Engineer (though that’s becoming a bit overused). More corporate versions would be AI Enablement, AI Adoption Specialist, or Learning & Development with an AI focus. Since your background is writing and strategy, “AI Writing Coach” or “AI Content Trainer” are also very searchable.”

Another thing Claude keeps doing is offering multiple choice options at the beginning of conversations. I’m still trying to figure out how to turn that off.

results.title: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files - only one made me nervous | ZDNET
results.content:
Cowork did struggle a bit, but that was while it was still in a research preview. I've used Cowork a lot since then, and it's performed without failure. I've also used ChatGPT's Codex agentic programming AI a lot since I first tested it out, and it's been enormously productive.

So, should you choose one over the other? Today, yes. If you're doing something potentially high stakes and you want to maintain oversight, use Claude Cowork. Full stop. But once OpenAI fixes the permissions issue (and I'm sure it will very quickly), I think it depends on whether you like OpenAI or Claude better.

Also:I tried Claude Cowork on my Gmail inbox after Gemini choked - and it saved me hours of work [...] Also: 1Password's new Agentic Mode lets Claude log into your accounts without seeing your credentials

One thing Claude Cowork had done that ChatGPT Work didn't do was to inform me that I had a bunch of very generically named files. I consider that a miss on the part of Work. Even so, I fed Work the same prompt I'd given to Cowork and let it run.

clean-names-prompt

Screenshot by David Gewirtz/ZDNET

As it churned, Work reported on the number of files it found and its observations. I liked that. It also talked about how it chose the files it wanted to rename. I found its reasoning valid. [...] That said, it's not bad. I did a fairly measurable amount of work using Codex last month fighting a server attack. While it did throttle me down a few times, I got the work done. Given the amount of work I did for my $20, I have no complaints.

I was definitely curious to see how much of my AI thinky allocation I used up on this file reorganization project.

usage.png

Screenshot by David Gewirtz/ZDNET

As you can see, when I started the project, I had 96% of my usage still available. A little over an hour later, I had 85%. I also have two resets available, which are essentially time bonuses OpenAI grants for a variety of fairly random reasons.

results.title: Recruitment Is Broken. Automation and Algorithms Can’t Fix It.
results.content:
“If applicants use ChatGPT to tailor a resume to a job description, employers are getting a whole lot of resumes that are basically the same,” Kohn said. “AI-enabled candidate matching is hurt, as well, because applicants are using AI to make themselves look like a much better fit than they actually are.”

Eubanks noted that new services allow candidates to pay small fees to automatically apply for jobs based on chosen criteria. “That is increasing the application volume for some employers, from thousands of resumes a month to thousands a day,” he said. [...] Job seekers struggle to stand out in processes increasingly mediated by machines that screen, rank, and interview candidates. Employers, meanwhile, are inundated with applicants leveraging AI-enabled tools to mass-apply, tailor resumes, and even auto-generate interview responses in real time.

Technology meant to streamline hiring — tools that have indeed delivered significant efficiencies — inadvertently created a monster of a process that’s at risk of eroding trust, fairness, and human judgment. For many, the hiring experience has become more frustrating, impersonal, and vulnerable to gaming.

According to the 2025 SHRM Benchmarking Survey, average cost-per-hire and time-to-hire have both increased in the past three years — a period correlating with increased use of generative AI.

## 😩 Why Interview Prep Is Broken (And Why AI Fixes It)

Interview prep hasn’t changed in a decade.

You refresh your resume. You Google “common [role] interview questions.” You run one mock interview with a friend who doesn’t know what the interviewer is actually looking for. You walk in, hope everything clicks, and walk out with a form rejection and zero feedback.

Three problems come up over and over:

The impostor spiral. You send out 20 applications and hear nothing. You start wondering: Is my resume broken? Am I actually not good enough? Without a feedback loop, you can’t tell. So you spiral. [...] The Product Channel By Sid Saladi

# The Product Channel By Sid Saladi

# Claude AI for Job Interviews 101: Your Complete System From First Application to Signed Offer

Sid Saladi's avatar

How to set up Claude as a personalized interview coach — and exactly what to do at every stage of the process.

Most people treat interviews like a test you either pass or fail.

You know your stuff. You’ve done the work. You show up and answer questions. And somehow, you still don’t get the job.

Here’s the thing nobody tells you: interviewing is a completely separate skill from being good at your job. The most qualified candidate in the room loses to the one who prepared better more often than anyone wants to admit. [...] After installing:

Open Claude, log in with your Pro account.

In the sidebar, go to Projects → Create Project → “Interview Coach.”

Go to Settings → Skills (or look for Skills in the sidebar — it may be labeled differently depending on your app version).

Create a new Skill named “Interview Coach.”

Paste in your SKILL.md content (the template in Step 2 below).

Save.

Your skill now activates automatically whenever you open your Interview Coach project. Claude will know your background, preferences, scoring rubrics, and session history without you saying anything.

Common setup issues:

“I don’t see Projects” → Make sure you’re logged into a Pro account.

“Skills isn’t showing” → Check Settings → Features and toggle it on.
